summary: Suggests additions to the Internet mail format of RFC 822 for a Content-Type header field, so that messages can say what kind of content they carry. It was a proposal for discussion and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A letter's envelope can say if it contains a photo or a drawing. This memo adds a label to email saying what type of thing is inside.

questions: what is the content-type header field
how did email first describe content types
what content types did rfc 1049 define
why was content-type proposed for email
subtitle: An early proposal for an email header that says how a message body is structured, such as PostScript or TROFF.

tldr.problem: Mail users were already sending TROFF, TeX or PostScript text inside ASCII messages, but the recipient had to notice this by eye and run the extra processing by hand.
tldr.mechanism: A new Content-Type header field names the structuring technique used in the body, with an optional version number, resource reference and comment, while the body itself stays plain ASCII as RFC 822 requires.
tldr.outcome: The memo asked for discussion and is now marked Historic. It deliberately left capability negotiation between sender and recipient for a later RFC.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: Up to four: type, version, resource reference, comment

facts.label: Initial types
facts.value: POSTSCRIPT, SCRIBE, SGML, TEX, TROFF, DVI, X-atom

facts.label: Case
facts.value: Type values are not case sensitive

today: RFC 1049 has the status Historic. It was a proposal for discussion and the unit metadata lists no newer RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Mail Needed a Content Type
sections.content:
An RFC 822 message has structured header fields (date, addresses) and a body that is just an unstructured string of ASCII characters. People were already using mail to send documents with embedded TROFF commands or encoded in a page description language such as PostScript. Showing those characters as plain text does not produce the page the sender meant; an extra processing step is needed.

This memo, an April 1988 request for discussion, proposes a new header field, Content-type:, as the standard way to say what structuring technique the body uses. A capable mail reader could then run the right processing automatically. Some systems already used private X- header fields for this, but wide use needs agreement on one name and its allowed values.

The body must still contain only the ASCII characters RFC 822 allows. For that reason the proposal should have no impact on existing mailers, only on mail reading systems. It also rules out octet-oriented encodings such as the Abstract Syntax Notation used in X.400.
sections.plainLanguage: People were already mailing special documents, but the reader had to guess what they were. A label on the message lets the mail program do the right thing for you.

sections.title: Problems with Structured Messages
sections.content:
Some receiving systems can process a structured body and some cannot. Because the body is limited to ASCII, a system that cannot process it will not break, but the result on screen may be hard for a person to read. If the sender used PostScript to get italics, boldface or Greek letters, there may be no ASCII equivalent at all.

The memo lists three ways to hide these differences from the sender: each mail system keeps a database of remote capabilities; the mail transport negotiates capabilities with the receiving system; or a directory service records the mail processing capabilities of hosts. Each needs changes (the database is hard to keep current, negotiation needs changes to all SMTP implementations and fails over networks that do not use SMTP, and the directory approach needs changes to mailers and to the domain name directory service). The memo notes that X.400 implements the second approach.

The author chooses to recommend none of them for now, so structured messages can start to be used early. A later RFC was to propose a solution based on negotiation. Until then, users must keep their own list of what recipients can handle, or the recipient sees raw PostScript or TROFF.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every friend has the same tools to open a fancy file. The memo says to keep the plan simple for now: know what your friend can open before you send it.

sections.title: The Content-type Header Field
sections.content:
The field has up to four parts: a type naming the structuring technique, an optional version number (ver-num), a resource reference (resource-ref) and a comment. In the RFC 822 notation it is Content-Type:= type [";" ver-num [";" 1#resource-ref]] [comment].

The initial type values are POSTSCRIPT, SCRIBE, SGML, TEX, TROFF and DVI, plus any private value beginning with X-. Values are not case sensitive. Both sender and recipient must know the technique precisely, so values should name a well-defined, standardized technique, although private ones known only to the two parties are not forbidden.

Version numbers depend on the type. The memo lists 1.0, 2.0 or null for PostScript, 3, 4, 5 or null for Scribe, and IS.8879.1986 or null for SGML.

The resource reference points to a well-known resource to use when processing, much as a LaserPrep file of font and macro definitions makes documents sent to a Laserwriter more compact. Proposed values are laserprep2.9, laserprep3.0, laserprep3.1 and laserprep4.0 for PostScript, and eqn, tbl and me for TROFF, in each case or a local part. The comment is free text in parentheses, as in RFC 822.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has a kind of document, maybe a version number, maybe a note about extra helper files, and a free comment. It is like writing Recipe, 2nd edition, uses the red cookbook.

sections.title: Conclusion and New Type Values
sections.content:
The memo repeats that a mail reading system need not take any action on seeing a valid Content-Type field. Recognizing it and invoking the right display process will improve readability and allow messages with mathematical symbols or foreign language characters. In the near term, the memo expects the main use to be marking a body as a page description language such as PostScript.

Additional type values are to be registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Coordinator at USC-ISI.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading the label is optional, but programs that do will show your messages better. New kinds of labels get written down in one official list.

references.text: Crocker, David H. RFC-822: Standard for the Format of ARPA Internet Text Messages. Network Information Center, August 13, 1982.
